components.note: 山 (mountain) — depicts a mountain, marking the character as related to mountains or great height.
魏 (wèi) gives a sound close to 巍's reading wēi — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这座山看起来很巍峨。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò shān kànqǐlái hěn wēi'é.
example.english: This mountain looks towering and majestic.
example.fact: Mount Everest, the world's tallest peak above sea level, rises about 8,849 meters — the kind of height 巍峨 (wēi'é, 'towering') describes.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
吾 (wú) gives the sound — an exact match with 唔's reading.

example.hanzi: 他想了想，唔了一声。
example.pinyin: Tā xiǎngle xiǎng, wúle yì shēng.
example.english: He thought for a moment and made a soft 'hmm' sound.
example.fact: In Cantonese, 唔 (m4) is the everyday word for 'not,' equivalent to Mandarin 不 — but in standard Mandarin it's mainly just a hesitation sound, not a negation word.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — the sickness radical, depicting a person lying on a sickbed — marking the character as related to illness.
久 (jiǔ) gives a sound close to 疚's reading jiù — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他觉得很内疚。
example.pinyin: Tā juéde hěn nèijiù.
example.english: He feels very guilty.
example.fact: 疚 pairs the 'sickness' radical 疒 with 久 ('a long time'), reflecting an old idea that prolonged guilt or sorrow could linger like a chronic illness.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — depicts a fish, marking the character as related to fish or aquatic creatures.
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 鲤's reading.

example.hanzi: 湖里有很多鲤鱼。
example.pinyin: Hú lǐ yǒu hěn duō lǐyú.
example.english: There are many carp in the lake.
example.fact: The idiom 鲤鱼跳龙门 ('a carp leaps over the dragon gate') comes from a legend of a carp transforming into a dragon, and is still used today for overcoming great odds to succeed.

etymologyHint: A hand holding a lance 戈

components.note: 戈 depicts a dagger-axe, a bladed weapon mounted on a pole. Combined with a now-obscure second component (likely representing armor), the pair of 'weapons and armor' together gave 戎 its meaning of arms and military affairs collectively.

example.hanzi: 古代士兵身披戎装上阵。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài shìbīng shēn pī róngzhuāng shàngzhèn.
example.english: Ancient soldiers went into battle wearing military uniforms.
example.fact: 戎 originally represented weapons and armor together, and today survives mainly in classical-sounding words like 从戎 ('to join the army') and 戎装 ('military attire').

components.note: 户 depicts a door or window.

攵 shows a hand holding a stick, indicating an action of striking. Together with 'door,' the image of forcing a door open came to represent starting or initiating something, giving 肇 its meaning 'to begin, commence.'

example.hanzi: 这场事故的肇事者已经被找到了。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng shìgù de zhàoshìzhě yǐjīng bèi zhǎodào le.
example.english: The person who caused this accident has already been found.
example.fact: 肇 gives its name to Zhaoqing (肇庆), a city in Guangdong province with over 2,000 years of recorded history.

components.note: 马 depicts a horse. 笃 was inspired by the steady, plodding gait and sound of a horse's hooves, which came to symbolize something solid, genuine, and sincere.

example.hanzi: 她笃信佛教。
example.pinyin: Tā dǔxìn Fójiào.
example.english: She firmly believes in Buddhism.
example.fact: 笃's bottom component, 马 (horse), hints at the character's roots in describing a horse's steady, plodding gait — an image extended to mean 'steadfast, sincere.'

meanings: rut; track of a wheel (Taiwan pr. [che4])
a rhyme (of a song, poem etc)
etymologyHint: Something left 育 by a cart 车 when it moves 攵

components.note: 车 depicts a cart or wagon.
攵 shows a hand with a stick, here suggesting motion. Together with 'cart,' the character evokes the tracks a moving wagon leaves behind, giving 辙 its meaning 'wagon rut, wheel track.'

example.hanzi: 我真是没辙了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zhēnshi méi zhé le.
example.english: I really have no solution — I'm at my wit's end.
example.fact: The idiom 南辕北辙 ('heading south while the wheel-ruts point north') describes acting against one's own stated goal; it comes from a Warring States-era story about a man traveling toward Chu while insisting the state lay to the north.

components.note: 女 (woman) — the woman radical, marking the character as related to a woman or a feminine quality.
闲 (xián) gives the sound — an exact match with 娴's reading.

example.hanzi: 她的动作十分娴熟。
example.pinyin: Tā de dòngzuò shífēn xiánshú.
example.english: Her movements are extremely skillful.
example.fact: 娴 pairs the 'woman' radical 女 with the phonetic component 闲 (xián, 'leisure'), reflecting an old association between cultivated leisure and elegant, skillful manners.

components.note: 元 (yuán) gives a sound related to 阮's reading ruǎn — they share the final -uan, though the initial consonant differs.

example.hanzi: 他会弹阮。
example.pinyin: Tā huì tán ruǎn.
example.english: He can play the ruan (a traditional Chinese lute).
example.fact: The ruan (阮) is a round-bodied plucked lute believed to be named after Ruan Xian, a 3rd-century musician among the 'Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove,' and it remains a core instrument in modern Chinese orchestras.

meanings: a kind of official document (in former times)

components.note: 木 (wood) points to the original writing surface: before paper was widespread, letters and official documents (札) were written on thin wooden slats.

example.hanzi: 他收到一封书札。
example.pinyin: Tā shōudào yì fēng shūzhá.
example.english: He received a letter.
example.fact: Before paper became widespread, Chinese letters and documents (札) were often written on thin wooden or bamboo slips — a history preserved in the character's 木 (wood) component.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the heart radical, marking the character as related to emotions or mental states.
奥 (ào) gives the sound — an exact match with 懊's reading.

example.hanzi: 他懊悔自己的选择。
example.pinyin: Tā àohuǐ zìjǐ de xuǎnzé.
example.english: He regrets his choice.
example.fact: 懊 almost always appears in the compound 懊悔 ('to regret') or 懊恼 ('annoyed, upset') — it essentially never stands alone in modern Mandarin.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — a form of 火 (fire) used at the bottom of characters, marking a connection to fire or heat.
寿 (shòu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 焘's reading dào.

example.hanzi: 他的名字里有一个'焘'字。
example.pinyin: Tā de míngzi lǐ yǒu yí gè 'dào' zì.
example.english: His name contains the character 'dào' (焘).
example.fact: 焘 is rare in everyday vocabulary today and survives mainly as a character in personal given names, such as that of the Southern Song historian Li Tao (李焘).

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the heart radical, marking the character as related to emotions or mental states.
血 (xuè) gives a sound close to 恤's reading xù, sharing the same initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 公司很体恤员工。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī hěn tǐxù yuángōng.
example.english: The company is very considerate toward its employees.
example.fact: 恤 is also used to transliterate the English word 'shirt' in the common loanword T恤 (T-xù, 'T-shirt'), found throughout the Chinese-speaking world.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — the sickness radical, depicting a person lying on a sickbed — marking the character as related to illness.
㐱 (zhěn) gives the sound — an exact match with 疹's reading; this rare character survives mainly as a phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 他身上起了湿疹。
example.pinyin: Tā shēnshang qǐle shīzhěn.
example.english: He developed a rash (eczema) on his skin.
example.fact: The measles vaccine, first licensed in 1963, has prevented tens of millions of deaths worldwide from a disease (麻疹) that was once nearly universal among children.

meanings: sound of beating wind and rain

components.note: 氵 (water) — the water radical, marking the character as related to water or liquid.
萧 (xiāo) gives the sound — an exact match with 潇's reading.

example.hanzi: 他穿得很潇洒。
example.pinyin: Tā chuān de hěn xiāosǎ.
example.english: He dresses in a carefree, stylish way.
example.fact: 潇 also names the Xiao River (潇水) in Hunan, whose confluence with the Xiang River gives the classical place name 潇湘 — a name often evoked in Chinese poetry for its misty, elegant scenery.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — the metal radical, marking the character as related to metal or metalworking.
吕 (lǚ) gives the sound — an exact match with 铝's reading.

example.hanzi: 这个锅是铝做的。
example.pinyin: Zhège guō shì lǚ zuò de.
example.english: This pot is made of aluminum.
example.fact: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, making up about 8% of it by mass, yet it wasn't isolated in pure form until 1825 because it's so difficult to extract from its ore.

components.note: 氵 (water) — the water radical, marking the character as related to water or liquid.
条 (tiáo) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 涤's reading dí.

example.hanzi: 洗涤剂可以去除污渍。
example.pinyin: Xǐdíjì kěyǐ qùchú wūzì.
example.english: Detergent can remove stains.
example.fact: 涤纶 (dílún), built on this character, is the Chinese name for polyester — one of the most widely produced synthetic fibers in the world.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the heart radical, marking the character as related to emotions or mental states.
寺 (sì) gives a sound close to 恃's reading shì, sharing the same final and a similar consonant.

example.hanzi: 他有恃无恐地做了这件事。
example.pinyin: Tā yǒushìwúkǒng de zuòle zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He did this fearlessly, confident he had backing.
example.fact: The idiom 有恃无恐 ('having support, thus no fear') comes from the Zuo Zhuan, a classical Chinese historical chronicle dating to around the 4th century BCE.

meanings: (bound form) subordinates in a gang of bandits

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
娄 (lóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 喽's reading.

example.hanzi: 山上有一群喽啰。
example.pinyin: Shān shàng yǒu yì qún lóuluo.
example.english: There is a group of underlings up on the mountain.
example.fact: 喽啰 (lóuluo) described the low-ranking followers of bandits or warlords in classical novels like Water Margin, and it's still used today to mean 'minions' or 'flunkies.'

meanings: to build by laying bricks or stones
etymologyHint: To cut 切 stone 石; 切 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 石 depicts stone or rock.
切 means 'to cut'; combined with 'stone,' cutting and fitting stones together extended to mean building or paving with them, as in stone steps.

example.hanzi: 工人正在砌墙。
example.pinyin: Gōngrén zhèngzài qì qiáng.
example.english: The workers are building a wall.
example.fact: The Great Wall of China, one of the largest construction projects in human history, was built over centuries using exactly the kind of stone- and brick-laying (砌) this character describes.

etymologyHint: To escape 辶 to shelter 盾; 盾 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 辶 (a walking/movement component) indicates motion — here, fleeing.
盾 means 'shield' and is pronounced dùn — the same sound as 遁 — hinting at a phonetic role, while also evoking hiding behind a shield; both point to 遁's meaning 'to escape, hide.'

example.hanzi: 犯人趁乱逃遁了。
example.pinyin: Fànrén chèn luàn táodùn le.
example.english: The criminal fled amid the chaos.
example.fact: 遁 appears in 奇门遁甲 (qímén dùnjiǎ), the name of an ancient Chinese system of divination and military strategy dating back over a thousand years.

meanings: used for Ceylon in Buddhist texts

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — the tree/wood radical, marking the character as related to trees, wood, or wooden objects.
罒 forms part of the phonetic element together with 方 (fāng) in the full character; on its own it has no strong independent reading, so its contribution to léng's sound is only partial.

example.hanzi: 他在读《楞严经》。
example.pinyin: Tā zài dú 《Léngyán Jīng》.
example.english: He is reading the Śūrangama Sūtra.
example.fact: 楞 appears mainly today in Buddhist scripture names transliterated from Sanskrit, such as 楞严经 (the Śūrangama Sūtra) — a reminder that some characters were repurposed purely for their sound to render foreign terms.

etymologyHint: A farm 阝 with a well 井; 井 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: On the left side, 阝 derives from 阜 (mound, earthworks), pointing to something dug into the ground.
井 means 'well' and is pronounced jǐng — the same as 阱 — evoking a deep pit dug into the earth like a well, which gave 阱 its meaning 'pitfall, trap.'

example.hanzi: 小心，前面有陷阱！
example.pinyin: Xiǎoxīn, qiánmiàn yǒu xiànjǐng!
example.english: Careful, there's a trap ahead!
example.fact: 阱 shares its phonetic component with 井 (jǐng, 'well') because both describe a deep pit dug into the ground — one for water, one to trap prey.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
处 (chù) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 咎's reading jiù.

example.hanzi: 这次失败完全是咎由自取。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì shībài wánquán shì jiùyóuzìqǔ.
example.english: This failure was entirely his own fault, brought on himself.
example.fact: 咎 appears throughout the ancient Yijing (Book of Changes) in the recurring judgment 无咎 ('no blame'), one of the text's most common verdicts on a hexagram line.

components.note: 氵 (water) — the water radical, marking the character as related to water or liquid.

圭 (guī) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 洼's reading wā — though the same 圭 phonetic series also produced 蛙 (wā, 'frog'), so the 'wa' sound is not a coincidence, just a very old one.

example.hanzi: 路上有一个水洼。
example.pinyin: Lù shàng yǒu yí gè shuǐwā.
example.english: There is a puddle on the road.
example.fact: The shore of the Dead Sea, at about 430 meters below sea level, is the lowest dry-land elevation on Earth — an extreme example of the low-lying '洼地' this character describes.

components.note: 火 (fire) — the fire radical, marking the character as related to fire, heat, or burning.
丙 (bǐng) gives the sound — an exact match with 炳's reading.

example.hanzi: 他的功绩彪炳史册。
example.pinyin: Tā de gōngjì biāobǐng shǐcè.
example.english: His achievements shine gloriously in the annals of history.
example.fact: 炳 is a popular character in Chinese given names, chosen for its bright, auspicious meaning — much like how English names sometimes draw on words meaning 'bright' or 'shining.'

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
筮 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 噬's reading.

example.hanzi: 鲨鱼张开嘴想吞噬猎物。
example.pinyin: Shāyú zhāngkāi zuǐ xiǎng tūnshì lièwù.
example.english: The shark opened its mouth, wanting to devour its prey.
example.fact: 反噬 ('to bite back') is a common Chinese word for a plan, tool, or ally that eventually turns destructively against its own creator.

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — the tree/wood radical, marking the character as related to trees, wood, or wooden objects.
风 (fēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 枫's reading.

example.hanzi: 秋天枫叶变红了。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān fēngyè biàn hóng le.
example.english: In autumn, the maple leaves turn red.
example.fact: The maple leaf is the national symbol of Canada and appears on its flag, though the sugar maple most associated with Canada differs from the maple species 枫 traditionally referred to in China.

meanings: (computing) to copy (abbr. for 拷貝|拷贝[kao3 bei4])
etymologyHint: To question 考 by hand 扌; 考 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action is done by hand, here striking or applying force.
考 means 'to examine, question' and is pronounced kǎo — identical to 拷 — linking the idea of forcing someone to answer questions with physical force, i.e. torture or interrogation.

example.hanzi: 请把这个文件拷贝一份。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ zhège wénjiàn kǎobèi yí fèn.
example.english: Please make a copy of this file.
example.fact: 拷贝 (kǎobèi) is a phonetic transliteration of the English word 'copy,' borrowed into Chinese in the early 20th century alongside film and technology terminology.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
多 (duō) gives the sound — an exact match with 哆's reading.

example.hanzi: 他冷得直哆嗦。
example.pinyin: Tā lěng de zhí duōsuo.
example.english: He was shivering from the cold.
example.fact: 哆嗦 (duōsuo) is one of many Chinese words built partly for sound, mimicking the visible shaking of a person shivering.

components.note: 石 (stone) — the stone radical, marking the character as related to rock or stone.
几 (jǐ) gives a sound close to 矶's reading jī — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 船只小心避开江边的矶石。
example.pinyin: Chuánzhī xiǎoxīn bìkāi jiāngbiān de jīshí.
example.english: Boats carefully avoid the rocky outcrops along the river.
example.fact: 采石矶 (Cǎishí Jī), a rocky outcrop on the Yangtze River in Anhui, was the site of a decisive 12th-century naval battle where Song forces repelled a Jin dynasty invasion.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — the grass/plant radical, marking the character as related to plants or vegetation.
韦 (wéi) gives a sound close to 苇's reading wěi — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 河边长着很多芦苇。
example.pinyin: Hébiān zhǎngzhe hěn duō lúwěi.
example.english: Many reeds grow along the riverbank.
example.fact: Reeds are among the fastest-growing wetland plants and play a major role in filtering pollutants from water, which is why they're widely used in constructed wetlands for water treatment.

components.note: 羽 (feather/wing) — depicts a pair of feathers or wings, marking the character as related to birds or flight.
扁 (biǎn) gives a sound close to 翩's reading piān — they share the same final, and the initials b/p differ only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 蝴蝶翩翩飞舞。
example.pinyin: Húdié piānpiān fēiwǔ.
example.english: The butterflies flutter and dance gracefully.
example.fact: The idiom 风度翩翩 describes someone with graceful, elegant manners, borrowing the same fluttering imagery used for a butterfly's flight to describe refined human behavior.

components.note: 穴 (cave) — depicts a cave or hole, marking the character as related to a hollow or enclosed space.
至 (zhì) gives the sound — an exact match with 窒's reading.

example.hanzi: 浓烟让他几乎窒息。
example.pinyin: Nóngyān ràng tā jīhū zhìxī.
example.english: The thick smoke nearly suffocated him.
example.fact: Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it's colorless and odorless yet can cause suffocation (窒息) by binding to hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does.

components.note: 亻 (person) — the person radical, marking the character as describing a person, their role, or their behavior.
农 (nóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 侬's reading.

example.hanzi: 在上海话里，'侬'是'你'的意思。
example.pinyin: Zài Shànghǎihuà lǐ, 'nóng' shì 'nǐ' de yìsi.
example.english: In Shanghainese, 'nóng' means 'you.'
example.fact: In the Wu Chinese dialects spoken around Shanghai and Suzhou, 侬 is the everyday word for 'you' — a completely different meaning from the classical 'I' sense the character can also carry.

components.note: 革 (leather/hide) — means 'leather, hide', marking the character as related to leather or hide goods.
巴 (bā) gives a sound close to 靶's reading bǎ — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 士兵们在打靶练习。
example.pinyin: Shìbīngmen zài dǎbǎ liànxí.
example.english: The soldiers are doing target practice.
example.fact: 靶 combines the leather radical 革 with 巴, since early targets for archery and shooting practice were often made by stretching leather or hide over a frame.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — a form of 肉 (flesh, body), marking the character as related to a body part or bodily substance.
夷 (yí) gives the sound — an exact match with 胰's reading.

example.hanzi: 胰岛素可以帮助控制血糖。
example.pinyin: Yídǎosù kěyǐ bāngzhù kòngzhì xuètáng.
example.english: Insulin can help control blood sugar.
example.fact: Insulin, discovered in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best, is produced by clusters of cells in the pancreas (胰) called the islets of Langerhans — the source of the Chinese term 胰岛素, literally 'pancreas-island-substance.'

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — the grass/plant radical, marking the character as related to plants or vegetation.
无 (wú) gives the sound — an exact match with 芜's reading.

example.hanzi: 这篇文章内容芜杂。
example.pinyin: Zhè piān wénzhāng nèiróng wúzá.
example.english: This article's content is disorganized and cluttered.
example.fact: 芜 gives its name to Wuhu (芜湖, literally 'weed lake'), a major Yangtze River port city in Anhui with over 2,000 years of history.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — the silk/thread radical, marking the character as related to thread, textiles, or thin strands.
辛 (xīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 辫's reading biàn.

example.hanzi: 她把头发编成辫子。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ tóufa biānchéng biànzi.
example.english: She braided her hair into a plait.
example.fact: During the Qing dynasty, Han Chinese men were required to wear their hair in a queue (辫子) in the Manchu style — cutting one's braid became a powerful symbolic act of rejecting Qing rule during the 1911 revolution.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
豪 (háo) gives the sound — an exact match with 嚎's reading.

example.hanzi: 狼在夜里嚎叫。
example.pinyin: Láng zài yèlǐ háojiào.
example.english: The wolf howls at night.
example.fact: Wolves howl mainly to communicate location and reassemble the pack across long distances — a howl can be heard by other wolves several kilometers away depending on the terrain.

etymologyHint: A woman 女 branded 辛 as a slave

components.note: 辛 originally depicted a sharp tool used for tattooing or branding, associated with punishment and servitude.
女 depicts a woman; combined with the mark of servitude above, the character originally showed a woman marked as a servant, which came to mean 'concubine.'

example.hanzi: 在古代中国，妾的地位远低于正妻。
example.pinyin: Zài gǔdài Zhōngguó, qiè de dìwèi yuǎn dī yú zhèngqī.
example.english: In ancient China, a concubine's status was far lower than that of the primary wife.
example.fact: The Chinese concubinage system was formally outlawed under the 1950 Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — depicts a piece of cloth hanging down, as from a belt — the cloth radical.
晃 (huàng, also read huǎng) gives the sound — an exact match with 幌's reading.

example.hanzi: 这家公司只是洗钱的幌子。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī zhǐshì xǐqián de huǎngzi.
example.english: This company is just a front for money laundering.
example.fact: 幌子 originally referred to the cloth signs traditional Chinese shops hung outside to advertise their goods, much like tavern signs in medieval Europe, before it came to mean a 'front' for hidden activities.

meanings: used in 踉蹌|踉跄[liang4 qiang4]

components.note: 足 (foot) — the foot radical, marking the character as related to the foot, legs, or walking.
良 (liáng) gives the sound — an exact match with 踉's reading.

example.hanzi: 他喝多了，走路踉踉跄跄的。
example.pinyin: Tā hē duō le, zǒulù liàngliàngqiàngqiàng de.
example.english: He drank too much and was staggering as he walked.
example.fact: 踉 is read liáng on its own but shifts to liàng in the common word 踉跄 ('to stagger') — a good example of how a character's reading can change depending on the word it appears in.

meanings: to rent farmland from a landlord
etymologyHint: A person 亻 on the farm 田; 田 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) marks the character as concerning a person's role or occupation.
田 means 'field' and is pronounced tián, close to (though not identical to) diàn — evoking a person working the fields, giving 佃 its meaning 'tenant farmer.'

example.hanzi: 过去很多农民是地主的佃农。
example.pinyin: Guòqù hěn duō nóngmín shì dìzhǔ de diànnóng.
example.english: In the past, many farmers were tenant farmers for landlords.
example.fact: Redistributing farmland from landlords to tenant farmers (佃农) was a central policy of the early People's Republic of China after 1949, fundamentally reshaping rural land ownership.

meanings: used in 葫蘆|葫芦[hu2 lu5]

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — the grass/plant radical, marking the character as related to plants or vegetation.
胡 (hú) gives the sound — an exact match with 葫's reading.

example.hanzi: 他买了一个葫芦做的水瓢。
example.pinyin: Tā mǎile yí gè húlu zuò de shuǐpiáo.
example.english: He bought a water ladle made from a gourd.
example.fact: The bottle gourd is believed to be one of the first plants ever domesticated by humans, with evidence of its use as a container dating back over 10,000 years across multiple continents.

meanings: short name for Anhui 安徽[An1 hui1]

components.note: 白 (white) — means 'white', marking the character as related to whiteness or brightness.
完 (wán) gives a sound close to 皖's reading wǎn — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 黄山位于皖南地区。
example.pinyin: Huángshān wèiyú Wǎnnán dìqū.
example.english: Mount Huangshan is located in southern Anhui.
example.fact: 皖 is the official one-character abbreviation for Anhui province, used on its vehicle license plates, and it comes from Mount Wan (皖山), an ancient name for a mountain there.

etymologyHint: To pull 曳 by hand 扌; 曳 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action is done by hand.

曳 means 'to drag, pull' — its meaning carries directly into 拽. (拽 also has a separate literary reading yè, identical to 曳, though the reading tested here, zhuāi, is the common one meaning 'to throw.')

example.hanzi: 他把书包用力一拽，扔到床上。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shūbāo yònglì yī zhuāi, rēng dào chuáng shàng.
example.english: He forcefully flung his backpack, throwing it onto the bed.
example.fact: 拽 has three distinct readings depending on meaning: zhuāi ('to throw,' used here), zhuài ('to pull, drag,' the more common Mandarin reading), and yè (a literary variant identical to 曳, 'to trail').

components.note: 氵 (water) — the water radical, marking the character as related to water or liquid.
虑 (lǜ) gives the sound — an exact match with 滤's reading.

example.hanzi: 这个机器可以过滤水中的杂质。
example.pinyin: Zhège jīqì kěyǐ guòlǜ shuǐ zhōng de zázhì.
example.english: This machine can filter impurities out of water.
example.fact: The first modern water filtration systems for entire cities were built in early 19th-century Scotland, dramatically reducing waterborne diseases like cholera in urban populations.

components.note: 目 (eye) — the eye radical, marking the character as related to sight or the eyes.
采 (cǎi) gives the sound — an exact match with 睬's reading.

example.hanzi: 她生气了，谁都不理睬。
example.pinyin: Tā shēngqì le, shéi dōu bù lǐcǎi.
example.english: She got angry and wouldn't pay attention to anyone.
example.fact: 睬 appears almost only in the negated pattern 不理睬 ('to ignore, pay no attention') in modern Mandarin — it's rarely used on its own to express positively paying attention.

example.hanzi: 俞是一个常见的中国姓氏。
example.pinyin: Yú shì yí gè chángjiàn de Zhōngguó xìngshì.
example.english: Yu is a common Chinese surname.
example.fact: 俞 is the surname of Yu Minhong (俞敏洪), founder of New Oriental Education & Technology Group, one of China's largest private education companies.

example.hanzi: 他身上藏着一把匕首。
example.pinyin: Tā shēnshang cángzhe yì bǎ bǐshǒu.
example.english: He had a dagger hidden on him.
example.fact: The idiom 图穷匕见 ('when the map unrolls to its end, the dagger appears') comes from the famous 227 BCE assassination attempt on the King of Qin, later China's First Emperor, in which a dagger was hidden inside a rolled map.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — a form of 言 (speech), marking the character as related to talking or language.
旁 (páng) gives a sound close to 谤's reading bàng — they share the same final, and the initials b/p differ only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 他因诽谤罪被起诉。
example.pinyin: Tā yīn fěibàng zuì bèi qǐsù.
example.english: He was prosecuted for the crime of slander.
example.fact: Unlike in the United States, where defamation is almost always a civil matter, Chinese law allows serious cases of slander (诽谤) to be prosecuted as a criminal offense.

etymologyHint: To laugh 蚩 out loud 口; 蚩 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 口 (mouth) indicates the action involves the mouth or voice — laughing, jeering.
蚩 means 'foolish, ridiculous' and is pronounced chī — identical to 嗤 — combining with 'mouth' to mean laughing at or mocking someone.

example.hanzi: 大家对他的想法嗤之以鼻。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā duì tā de xiǎngfǎ chīzhībǐ.
example.english: Everyone scoffed disdainfully at his idea.
example.fact: The idiom 嗤之以鼻 literally means 'to snort through the nose at it,' using 嗤 (an onomatopoeia for a scornful snort) to vividly capture a gesture of contempt.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — the hand radical, marking the character as related to an action performed with the hand.
旱 (hàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 捍's reading.

example.hanzi: 军人捍卫国家的领土。
example.pinyin: Jūnrén hànwèi guójiā de lǐngtǔ.
example.english: Soldiers defend the nation's territory.
example.fact: 捍卫 is one of the most common words in Chinese political and legal writing, frequently paired with abstract nouns like 主权 ('sovereignty') and 权利 ('rights').

etymologyHint: To brood 孚 over eggs 卵

components.note: 卵 means 'egg' — it shows what is being hatched.
孚 originally depicted a hand over a child and means 'to brood over, to nurture'; it's pronounced fú, close to 孵's fū, reinforcing the meaning 'to hatch, incubate.'

example.hanzi: 母鸡正在孵蛋。
example.pinyin: Mǔjī zhèngzài fū dàn.
example.english: The hen is hatching (incubating) eggs.
example.fact: A domestic chicken egg typically takes about 21 days to hatch under constant incubation at around 37.5°C, whether by a broody hen or an artificial incubator.

components.note: 亻 (person) marks this as related to a person.
兒 (child) depicts a young child; combined with 'person,' the character evokes something small, young, or feeble.

example.hanzi: 警方终于看出了一些端倪。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhōngyú kànchūle yīxiē duānní.
example.english: The police finally spotted some clues.
example.fact: 端倪 combines 端 ('end, beginning') and 倪 ('edge, extremity') to mean the first visible sign of something larger — much like the English idiom 'the tip of the iceberg.'

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — the sickness radical, depicting a person lying on a sickbed — marking the character as related to illness.
隐 (yǐn) gives the sound — an exact match with 瘾's reading.

example.hanzi: 他打游戏打上瘾了。
example.pinyin: Tā dǎ yóuxì dǎ shàngyǐn le.
example.english: He got addicted to playing video games.
example.fact: The World Health Organization officially classified 'gaming disorder' as a recognized condition in its ICD-11 diagnostic manual in 2019, reflecting growing global concern over video game addiction.

components.note: 攵 (hand with a stick) — depicts a hand holding a stick or rod, suggesting striking or performing an action.

example.hanzi: 他穿着一件破敝的旧衣服。
example.pinyin: Tā chuānzhe yí jiàn pòbì de jiù yīfu.
example.english: He was wearing a worn-out old piece of clothing.
example.fact: 敝 is also used as a humble self-reference in classical and formal Chinese, as in 敝人 ('your humble servant,' i.e., 'me') — a convention where speakers deprecate themselves as a form of politeness.

components.note: 匚 (box/container) — depicts an open box or container.
王 (wáng) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 匡's reading kuāng.

example.hanzi: 他努力匡正社会上的不良风气。
example.pinyin: Tā nǔlì kuāngzhèng shèhuì shàng de bùliáng fēngqì.
example.english: He worked hard to correct bad social trends.
example.fact: The classical idiom 一匡天下 ('to bring order to the whole realm') describes rulers or statesmen who successfully unified and stabilized a fractured state.

meanings: (old) to polish bones, horns, ivory etc into tools

components.note: 石 (stone) — the stone radical, marking the character as related to rock or stone.
差 (chà/chā/cī) is the historical phonetic element; none of its readings closely match 磋's reading cuō today.

example.hanzi: 两位棋手互相切磋棋艺。
example.pinyin: Liǎng wèi qíshǒu hùxiāng qiēcuō qíyì.
example.english: The two chess players exchanged views to sharpen their skills.
example.fact: 切磋 originally described the literal process of cutting and polishing bone, horn, or jade into finished tools or ornaments — refining a raw material became a metaphor for people refining their skills together.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — the silk/thread radical, marking the character as related to thread, textiles, or thin strands.
夌 (líng) gives the sound — an exact match with 绫's reading; 夌 is the shared root behind other líng characters like 凌 and 陵.

example.hanzi: 她穿着绫罗绸缎，十分华丽。
example.pinyin: Tā chuānzhe língluóchóuduàn, shífēn huálì.
example.english: She was dressed in fine silks, extremely resplendent.
example.fact: 绫罗绸缎 is a four-character set phrase combining four different types of fine silk fabric, traditionally used in classical Chinese literature to describe luxurious clothing.

components.note: 氵 (water) — the water radical, marking the character as related to water or liquid.
肴 (yáo) gives a sound close to 淆's reading xiáo — they share the same final -iao.

example.hanzi: 别把这两个概念混淆了。
example.pinyin: Bié bǎ zhè liǎng gè gàiniàn hùnxiáo le.
example.english: Don't confuse these two concepts.
example.fact: 混淆 often appears in the phrase 混淆视听 ('to confuse public perception'), a standard term in Chinese legal and media writing for the deliberate spreading of misleading information.

components.note: 兀 means 'high, bare, prominent' (as in a bald mountaintop). The traditional form of this character, 堯, showed layers of earth 土 piled up high above this base — an image of loftiness — which became the name of the legendary sage-king Yao, renowned for his exalted virtue.

example.hanzi: 尧和舜是中国古代传说中的贤明君主。
example.pinyin: Yáo hé Shùn shì Zhōngguó gǔdài chuánshuō zhōng de xiánmíng jūnzhǔ.
example.english: Yao and Shun are wise rulers from ancient Chinese legend.
example.fact: Yao (尧) and his successor Shun (舜), legendary sage-kings said to have ruled around the 3rd millennium BCE, are traditionally celebrated in Confucian thought as models of virtuous rulers who chose successors based on merit rather than heredity.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — the grass/plant radical, marking the character as related to plants or vegetation.
惢 (ruǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 蕊's reading; this rare character (literally three 心 stacked) survives mainly as a phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 蜜蜂落在花蕊上采蜜。
example.pinyin: Mìfēng luò zài huāruǐ shàng cǎimì.
example.english: The bee lands on the flower's stamen to collect nectar.
example.fact: A flower's stamens produce pollen that must reach the pistil — together forming what 花蕊 refers to — for fertilization to occur, a process pollinators like bees are essential to.

components.note: 火 (fire) — the fire radical, marking the character as related to fire, heat, or burning.
共 (gòng) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 烘's reading hōng.

example.hanzi: 妈妈在烘焙面包。
example.pinyin: Māma zài hōngbèi miànbāo.
example.english: Mom is baking bread.
example.fact: 烘焙 (baking) has become an especially common word in mainland China since the 2000s, alongside the rapid growth of Western-style bakery cafes.

components.note: 王 (jade) — a form of 玉 (jade), marking the character as related to jade or a precious stone.
章 (zhāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 璋's reading.

example.hanzi: '弄璋之喜'是古人对生男孩的祝贺用语。
example.pinyin: 'Nòngzhāng zhī xǐ' shì gǔrén duì shēng nánhái de zhùhè yòngyǔ.
example.english: 'The joy of playing with a jade tablet' was an ancient expression congratulating the birth of a son.
example.fact: In ancient China, giving a baby boy a jade tablet (璋) to play with — and a baby girl a spindle-whorl — reflected traditional gender expectations, and 弄璋 became a poetic phrase for the birth of a son.

example.hanzi: 他情绪十分亢奋。
example.pinyin: Tā qíngxù shífēn kàngfèn.
example.english: He was extremely excited/overexcited.
example.fact: The idiom 不卑不亢 describes someone who is neither servile nor arrogant, striking a balanced, dignified manner — a virtue often praised in Chinese diplomatic and social etiquette.

components.note: 车 (cart) — depicts a cart or wagon, marking the character as related to vehicles.
乚 is a curled stroke with no independent reading of its own — it appears here as a graphic remnant rather than a true phonetic clue.

example.hanzi: 这家工厂负责轧钢。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngchǎng fùzé yàgāng.
example.english: This factory is responsible for rolling steel.
example.fact: 轧 has two common readings depending on the word: yà ('to crush, roll,' as in industrial steel-rolling) and zhá (in words like 轧账, 'to reconcile accounts').

components.note: 贝 depicts a cowrie shell, used as ancient currency — it marks the character as related to money or valuables.
各 means 'each, individual'; combined with 'money,' it evokes money changing hands to an individual, giving 赂 its meaning 'to bribe.'

example.hanzi: 他因贿赂官员被逮捕。
example.pinyin: Tā yīn huìlù guānyuán bèi dàibǔ.
example.english: He was arrested for bribing officials.
example.fact: The Tang Code, one of the earliest complete legal codes in Chinese history (7th century CE), already contained detailed provisions criminalizing bribery (贿赂) among officials.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — the insect radical, originally depicting a snake-like shape, marking the character as related to insects or small creatures.
皇 (huáng) gives the sound — an exact match with 蝗's reading.

example.hanzi: 蝗虫会大量啃食农作物。
example.pinyin: Huángchóng huì dàliàng kěnshí nóngzuòwù.
example.english: Locusts devour large quantities of crops.
example.fact: Desert locust swarms can contain billions of insects covering hundreds of square kilometers, and a single large swarm can eat as much food in a day as tens of thousands of people.

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — the tree/wood radical, marking the character as related to trees, wood, or wooden objects.
俞 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 榆's reading.

example.hanzi: 院子里种着一棵榆树。
example.pinyin: Yuànzi lǐ zhòngzhe yì kē yúshù.
example.english: An elm tree is planted in the courtyard.
example.fact: Elm trees were once common street trees across North America until Dutch elm disease, a fungal infection spread by bark beetles, killed tens of millions of elms starting in the 20th century.

components.note: 马 (horse) — depicts a horse, marking the character as related to horses.
夋 (qūn) gives a sound related to 骏's reading jùn: they share the final -un, and q/j is a common alternation between initials in phonetic series like this one.

example.hanzi: 将军骑着一匹骏马。
example.pinyin: Jiāngjūn qízhe yì pǐ jùnmǎ.
example.english: The general rode a fine steed.
example.fact: 骏 is a popular character in Chinese given names for boys, chosen for its connotation of strength and excellence.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — a form of 言 (speech), marking the character as related to talking or language.
朱 (zhū) gives the sound — an exact match with 诛's reading.

example.hanzi: 大家对他的行为口诛笔伐。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā duì tā de xíngwéi kǒuzhū bǐfá.
example.english: Everyone condemned his behavior in speech and writing.
example.fact: The idiom 口诛笔伐 ('to execute with the mouth, attack with the pen') describes strong public condemnation through words rather than actual violence.

etymologyHint: A spoon 勹 with something in it 丶

components.note: 勹 here forms the outline of a ladle or spoon; the dot inside represents its contents — together depicting a spoon.

example.hanzi: 他用勺子喝汤。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng sháozi hē tāng.
example.english: He drinks soup with a spoon.
example.fact: 勺 is also an old Chinese unit of volume, historically defined as one-tenth of a 合 (gě) — part of a volumetric system used before the metric system became standard.

meanings: abbr. for 梵教[Fan4 jiao4] Brahmanism
abbr. for 梵蒂岡|梵蒂冈[Fan4 di4 gang1], the Vatican

components.note: 林 (forest) — two 木 (tree) side by side, depicting a grove or forest.
凡 (fán) gives a sound close to 梵's reading fàn — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这本佛经是用梵文写的。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn fójīng shì yòng Fànwén xiě de.
example.english: This Buddhist sutra is written in Sanskrit.
example.fact: 梵 is a phonetic transliteration of 'Brahma,' and it became the standard character for anything related to ancient India or Sanskrit, from 梵文 (Sanskrit) to 梵蒂冈 (Fàndìgāng, 'Vatican').

components.note: 火 (fire) — the fire radical, marking the character as related to fire, heat, or burning.
只 (zhǐ) gives a sound close to 炽's reading chì — they share the same final, and the initials zh/ch differ only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 沙漠中午的阳光十分炽热。
example.pinyin: Shāmò zhōngwǔ de yángguāng shífēn chìrè.
example.english: The midday sun in the desert is scorching hot.
example.fact: The surface of the Sun is about 5,500°C, but its core reaches roughly 15 million°C — the blazing heat (炽热) driving the nuclear fusion that powers all sunlight.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — the bamboo radical, marking the character as related to bamboo or objects made of it.
立 (lì) gives the sound — an exact match with 笠's reading.

example.hanzi: 农民戴着斗笠在田里劳作。
example.pinyin: Nóngmín dàizhe dǒulì zài tián lǐ láozuò.
example.english: The farmer works in the field wearing a conical bamboo hat.
example.fact: The conical bamboo hat (斗笠) has been used across East and Southeast Asia for centuries as inexpensive, effective protection from sun and rain for farmers and laborers.

components.note: 页 (head) — depicts a kneeling person with an emphasized head, marking the character as related to the head or face.
合 (hé) gives the sound — an exact match with 颌's reading.

example.hanzi: 医生检查了他的下颌骨。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiǎnchále tā de xiàhégǔ.
example.english: The doctor examined his lower jawbone.
example.fact: The human jaw muscle (masseter) is, pound for pound, one of the strongest muscles in the body, capable of exerting a bite force of over 70 kilograms on the molars.

components.note: 门 (gate/door) — depicts a double door or gate, marking the character as related to doors, gates, or enclosures.
甲 (jiǎ) gives a sound close to 闸's reading zhá, sharing the same final.

example.hanzi: 工人打开了水闸放水。
example.pinyin: Gōngrén dǎkāile shuǐzhá fàngshuǐ.
example.english: The workers opened the sluice gate to release the water.
example.fact: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River, the largest hydroelectric power station in the world by installed capacity, relies on massive sluice gates (闸门) as part of its flood-control system.

components.note: 犭 (animal) — the dog/animal radical, marking the character as related to an animal.
弗 (fú) gives a sound close to 狒's reading fèi, sharing the same initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 动物园里有一群狒狒。
example.pinyin: Dòngwùyuán lǐ yǒu yì qún fèifèi.
example.english: There is a troop of baboons at the zoo.
example.fact: Baboons live in complex social troops that can number over 100 individuals, with a strict, often matrilineal, dominance hierarchy.

components.note: 大 (big) — hints at a large enclosed area, fitting 樊's meaning of a railing or fenced-in enclosure.
棥 (a rare component, historically read fán) gives the sound — an exact match with 樊's reading.

example.hanzi: 他觉得婚姻像一个樊笼。
example.pinyin: Tā juéde hūnyīn xiàng yí gè fánlóng.
example.english: He feels that marriage is like a cage.
example.fact: 樊 is also a common Chinese surname, borne notably by Fan Kuai (樊哙), a general and close companion of Liu Bang, founder of the Han dynasty.

etymologyHint: A mold that holds 容 hot metal 钅; 容 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) marks the character as related to metal or metalworking.
容 means 'to contain, hold' and is pronounced róng — identical to 镕 — evoking a mold that holds molten metal, giving 镕 its meaning 'to smelt, fuse.'

example.hanzi: 朱镕基曾任中国国务院总理。
example.pinyin: Zhū Róngjī céng rèn Zhōngguó Guówùyuàn Zǒnglǐ.
example.english: Zhu Rongji once served as Premier of China's State Council.
example.fact: 镕 is essentially a variant of the more common character 熔 (also róng, 'to melt/smelt') and today survives mainly in personal names, most notably that of former Chinese Premier Zhu Rongji.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — the earth radical, marking the character as related to soil, ground, or dirt.
后 (hòu) gives a sound close to 垢's reading gòu, sharing the same final.

example.hanzi: 这块布上有很多污垢。
example.pinyin: Zhè kuài bù shàng yǒu hěn duō wūgòu.
example.english: This piece of cloth has a lot of grime on it.
example.fact: The idiom 蓬头垢面 ('disheveled hair and a grimy face') is often used in classical Chinese literature to describe someone in deep distress or extreme poverty.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — the sickness radical, depicting a person lying on a sickbed — marking the character as related to illness.
昷 (wēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 瘟's reading; 昷 is the ancestor form behind 温 and 瘟 alike.

example.hanzi: 古代瘟疫经常造成大量人口死亡。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài wēnyì jīngcháng zàochéng dàliàng rénkǒu sǐwáng.
example.english: In ancient times, epidemics often caused massive loss of life.
example.fact: The Black Death, a bubonic plague pandemic in the 14th century, is estimated to have killed 30–60% of Europe's population and also devastated parts of Asia, making it one of the deadliest pandemics in human history.

meanings: used in 綢繆|绸缪[chou2 mou2]

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — the silk/thread radical, marking the character as related to thread, textiles, or thin strands.
翏 (liù) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 缪's reading móu.

example.hanzi: 我们应该未雨绸缪，提前做好准备。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi wèiyǔchóumóu, tíqián zuò hǎo zhǔnbèi.
example.english: We should plan ahead and prepare in advance, like tying things down before it rains.
example.fact: 缪 has three different readings depending on context: móu (as in 绸缪, 'to plan ahead'), miù (a variant of 谬, 'mistaken'), and Miào (a surname).

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — the grass/plant radical, marking the character as related to plants or vegetation.
姑 (gū) gives the sound — an exact match with 菇's reading.

example.hanzi: 妈妈买了一些香菇回来做饭。
example.pinyin: Māma mǎile yīxiē xiānggū huílái zuòfàn.
example.english: Mom bought some shiitake mushrooms to cook with.
example.fact: Shiitake mushrooms have been cultivated in China and Japan for over 1,000 years and are among the most widely cultivated edible mushrooms in the world today.

components.note: 王 (jade) — a form of 玉 (jade), marking the character as related to jade or a precious stone.
奇 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 琦's reading.

example.hanzi: 琦是一个常用在人名中的字。
example.pinyin: Qí shì yí gè chángyòng zài rénmíng zhōng de zì.
example.english: Qi is a character commonly used in personal names.
example.fact: 琦 shares its 'jade' radical 王 with dozens of other characters used in Chinese given names, since jade has symbolized purity and virtue in Chinese culture for thousands of years.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — a form of 刀 (knife), marking the character as related to cutting.
弟 (dì) gives a sound close to 剃's reading tì — they share the same final, and the initials d/t differ only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 他每天早上用剃须刀剃须。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān zǎoshang yòng tìxūdāo tìxū.
example.english: He shaves with a razor every morning.
example.fact: In the early Qing dynasty, the government ordered Han Chinese men to shave the sides of their heads and adopt the Manchu queue hairstyle, making the act of shaving (剃发) a politically loaded symbol of submission to the new regime.

components.note: 辶 (walk/move) — a form of 辵 (to walk), marking the character as related to movement or travel.
并 (bìng) gives a sound close to 迸's reading bèng, sharing the same initial and a similar nasal final.

example.hanzi: 火花从铁块上迸发出来。
example.pinyin: Huǒhuā cóng tiěkuài shàng bèngfā chūlái.
example.english: Sparks burst forth from the piece of iron.
example.fact: 迸发 is often used metaphorically in Chinese to describe a sudden burst of emotion or creativity, as in 灵感迸发 ('inspiration bursts forth').

components.note: 氵 (water) — the water radical, marking the character as related to water or liquid.
弱 (ruò) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 溺's reading nì.

example.hanzi: 很多父母溺爱自己的孩子。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō fùmǔ nì'ài zìjǐ de háizi.
example.english: Many parents excessively dote on their children.
example.fact: 溺爱 uses the same character as 'drowning' (溺水) to convey love so excessive it overwhelms a child, much like water overwhelms someone who drowns.

meanings: (bound form) to boast; to show off

components.note: 火 (fire) — the fire radical, marking the character as related to fire, heat, or burning.
玄 (xuán) gives a sound close to 炫's reading xuàn — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他喜欢在朋友面前炫耀自己的新车。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan zài péngyou miànqián xuànyào zìjǐ de xīn chē.
example.english: He likes to show off his new car in front of friends.
example.fact: The slang term 炫富 ('to flaunt wealth') became a widely discussed phenomenon on Chinese social media in the 2010s, describing influencers who publicly displayed luxury goods to gain followers.

etymologyHint: To neglect 忽 the mind 忄; 忽 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) shows the character relates to a mental or emotional state.
忽 means 'to neglect, suddenly' and is pronounced hū — identical to 惚 — together describing a distracted, absent-minded state of mind, as in 恍惚 (huǎnghū, 'in a daze').

example.hanzi: 他大病之后，精神一直很恍惚。
example.pinyin: Tā dà bìng zhīhòu, jīngshén yīzhí hěn huǎnghū.
example.english: After his serious illness, he has remained mentally dazed.
example.fact: 恍惚 appears in the opening lines of the Dao De Jing, describing the Dao itself as vague and elusive ('恍兮惚兮') — one of the oldest philosophical uses of this pair of characters.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
海 (hǎi) gives a sound close to 嗨's reading hāi — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他一见到我就说：'嗨，你好！'
example.pinyin: Tā yī jiàndào wǒ jiù shuō: 'Hāi, nǐ hǎo!'
example.english: As soon as he saw me, he said, 'Hi, hello!'
example.fact: 嗨 as a casual greeting is a relatively recent loanword usage in Mandarin, borrowed from English 'hi' — distinct from its older meaning as an exclamation of dismay.

meanings: (bound form) to fall from the sky

components.note: 阝 (mound/place) — on the left side, a form of 阜 (mound, earthworks), often relating to terrain, elevation, or place.
员 (yuán) gives a sound close to 陨's reading yǔn, sharing the same initial.

example.hanzi: 科学家在沙漠里发现了一块陨石。
example.pinyin: Kēxuéjiā zài shāmò lǐ fāxiànle yí kuài yǔnshí.
example.english: Scientists discovered a meteorite in the desert.
example.fact: The 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor, which exploded over Russia, released energy equivalent to roughly 20-30 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs and injured over 1,000 people, mostly from shattered glass.

components.note: 贝 (cowrie shell/money) — depicts a cowrie shell, used as ancient currency, marking the character as related to money or valuables.
庄 (zhuāng) gives a sound close to 赃's reading zāng, sharing the same final and closely related initials (z/zh).

example.hanzi: 警方查获了一批赃物。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng cháhuòle yì pī zāngwù.
example.english: The police seized a batch of stolen goods.
example.fact: The idiom 贪赃枉法 ('to embezzle and pervert the law') is a standard phrase in Chinese anti-corruption discourse for officials who take bribes in exchange for abusing their power.

etymologyHint: A leather 革 halter used to control 罒a horse  马

components.note: 革 means 'leather, hide' — the material of a bridle or halter.
马 depicts a horse; combined with leather (and a net-like top element suggesting binding), the character evokes a leather halter used to control a horse, giving 羁 its meaning 'to restrain, hold back.'

example.hanzi: 他生性放荡不羁。
example.pinyin: Tā shēngxìng fàngdàng bù jī.
example.english: He is unrestrained and free-spirited by nature.
example.fact: 羁旅 ('a restrained journey,' i.e. travel far from home) is a recurring theme in classical Chinese poetry, expressing the homesickness felt by travelers and exiled officials.

components.note: 至 (arrive) — depicts an arrow striking the ground, meaning 'to arrive, reach' — it carries the idea of reaching an endpoint.
秦 (qín) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 臻's reading zhēn.

example.hanzi: 这项技术已经日臻完善。
example.pinyin: Zhè xiàng jìshù yǐjīng rìzhēn wánshàn.
example.english: This technology has become increasingly refined day by day.
example.fact: 臻 is a popular character in Chinese business and brand names for its connotation of reaching an ideal, perfected state.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
啇 (dí) gives the sound — an exact match with 嘀's reading; this component also underlies 敵/敌 and 摘.

example.hanzi: 他一个人在那儿嘀咕什么。
example.pinyin: Tā yí gè rén zài nàr dígu shénme.
example.english: He's over there muttering something to himself.
example.fact: 嘀咕 is an onomatopoeic-feeling word, similar to how English uses 'mutter' or 'mumble' to imitate the low, indistinct sound of quiet talking.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — a form of 肉 (flesh, body), marking the character as related to a body part or bodily substance.
善 (shàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 膳's reading.

example.hanzi: 医生建议他注意膳食均衡。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiànyì tā zhùyì shànshí jūnhéng.
example.english: The doctor advised him to pay attention to a balanced diet.
example.fact: 御膳房, the Imperial Kitchen, was the department responsible for preparing meals for the emperor within the Forbidden City, staffed by hundreds of cooks specializing in different regional and ceremonial cuisines.

meanings: abbr. for Jiangxi Province 江西省[Jiang1 xi1 Sheng3]

components.note: 夂 depicts a trailing footstep/foot, suggesting movement; it's a structural remnant of the character's complex traditional form 贛, only loosely tied to 赣's meaning today.
贡 (gòng) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 赣's reading gàn.

example.hanzi: 赣江是江西省最大的河流。
example.pinyin: Gàn Jiāng shì Jiāngxī Shěng zuìdà de héliú.
example.english: The Gan River is the largest river in Jiangxi province.
example.fact: 赣 is the official one-character abbreviation for Jiangxi province, and at 21 strokes it is one of the most complex characters used for any Chinese province name.

meanings: used in 躊躇|踌躇[chou2 chu2]

components.note: 足 (foot) — the foot radical, marking the character as related to the foot, legs, or walking.
寿 (shòu) gives a sound close to 踌's reading chóu, sharing the same final -ou, with sh/ch being closely related retroflex consonants.

example.hanzi: 他升职后踌躇满志。
example.pinyin: Tā shēngzhí hòu chóuchú mǎnzhì.
example.english: After his promotion, he was smugly pleased with his success.
example.fact: 踌躇 can mean both 'to hesitate' and, in the fixed idiom 踌躇满志, 'smug satisfaction' — an example of how the same compound can shift meaning depending on the surrounding phrase.

meanings: to be buried with the dead

components.note: 歹 (death/misfortune) — originally depicted broken, fragmented bones, marking the character as related to death or misfortune.
旬 (xún) gives a sound close to 殉's reading xùn — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 这位消防员因公殉职。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi xiāofángyuán yīn gōng xùnzhí.
example.english: This firefighter died in the line of duty.
example.fact: The Qin terracotta army is believed by many historians to have been created partly as a substitute for the earlier, harsher practice of burying living attendants (殉葬) alongside a ruler.

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — the tree/wood radical, marking the character as related to trees, wood, or wooden objects.
吉 (jí) gives a sound close to 桔's reading jú, sharing the same initial.

example.hanzi: 冬天吃桔子对身体好。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān chī júzi duì shēntǐ hǎo.
example.english: Eating tangerines in winter is good for your health.
example.fact: 桔 is a variant character commonly used in place of 橘 for 'tangerine' in everyday writing, even though its original classical meaning refers to the unrelated medicinal herb 桔梗 (jiégěng, balloon flower).

etymologyHint: A bird 隹 with two wide eyes 目

components.note: 目 (eye) is doubled here to show wide, staring eyes.
隹 depicts a short-tailed bird, such as a hawk; a bird with wide, staring eyes evokes a startled, alert gaze, which gave 瞿 its meaning 'startled.' It's also a common surname.

example.hanzi: 瞿秋白是中国共产党早期的重要领导人。
example.pinyin: Qú Qiūbái shì Zhōngguó Gòngchǎndǎng zǎoqī de zhòngyào lǐngdǎorén.
example.english: Qu Qiubai was an important early leader of the Chinese Communist Party.
example.fact: Qu Qiubai (瞿秋白, 1899–1935) was a leading Chinese revolutionary and writer, and one of the party's early leaders before being executed by Nationalist forces.

meanings: short name for Fujian 福建[Fu2 jian4]

components.note: 虫 (insect) — the insect radical, originally depicting a snake-like shape, marking the character as related to insects or small creatures.
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 闽's reading mǐn, sharing the same initial.

example.hanzi: 闽南话是福建南部的方言。
example.pinyin: Mǐnnánhuà shì Fújiàn nánbù de fāngyán.
example.english: Minnan (Southern Min) is a dialect spoken in southern Fujian.
example.fact: 闽 is the official abbreviation for Fujian province, and the Min Chinese dialects it names, including Hokkien, are considered some of the most internally diverse branches of Chinese.

etymologyHint: A pig 豕 suckling at its mother's teat ⺼

components.note: 豕 depicts a pig.
⺼ (flesh) here alludes to a suckling piglet nursing at its mother, giving 豚 its meaning 'small, suckling pig.'

example.hanzi: 河豚有毒，要小心处理。
example.pinyin: Hétún yǒudú, yào xiǎoxīn chǔlǐ.
example.english: Pufferfish are poisonous and must be handled carefully.
example.fact: The pufferfish contains tetrodotoxin, a neurotoxin far more potent than cyanide, yet it remains a prized delicacy in Japan (as fugu) and parts of China, prepared only by specially licensed chefs.

meanings: to mix; to blend; to dilute; to adulterate

components.note: 扌 (hand) — the hand radical, marking the character as related to an action performed with the hand.

参 (here read cān) gives a sound close to 掺's reading càn — the same syllable, differing only in tone; càn is a rare classical reading found mainly in the drum-music term 渔阳掺, distinct from 掺's far more common reading chān ('to mix').

example.hanzi: 《渔阳掺》是一首古代的鼓曲。
example.pinyin: 《Yúyáng Càn》 shì yì shǒu gǔdài de gǔqǔ.
example.english: 'Yuyang Can' is an ancient drum piece.
example.fact: 掺 usually reads chān and means 'to mix, blend,' but it has a separate, much rarer reading, càn, found only in the ancient drum-rhythm term 渔阳掺.

components.note: 氵 (water) — the water radical, marking the character as related to water or liquid.
屯 (tún) gives a sound close to 沌's reading dùn, sharing the same final, with initials t/d differing only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 中国神话中，世界最初是一片混沌。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó shénhuà zhōng, shìjiè zuìchū shì yí piàn hùndùn.
example.english: In Chinese mythology, the world was originally a state of chaos.
example.fact: The idea of 混沌 (primordial chaos) appears in the early Daoist text Zhuangzi, which describes a formless being named Hundun — a philosophical precursor to later Chinese creation myths.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the heart radical, marking the character as related to emotions or mental states.
左 (zuǒ) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 惰's reading duò.

example.hanzi: 他做事很懒惰。
example.pinyin: Tā zuòshì hěn lǎnduò.
example.english: He is very lazy about doing things.
example.fact: The Chinese term for physical inertia is 惯性, but a related older term, 惰性 (literally 'laziness-nature'), also describes a body's natural tendency to resist change — the same root idea appearing in both physical and behavioral contexts.

meanings: used in 喳喳[cha1 cha1] and 喳喳[cha1 cha5]

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
查 (chá) gives a sound close to 喳's reading zhā, sharing the same final and closely related initials (ch/zh).

example.hanzi: 小鸟在树上喳喳地叫。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo niǎo zài shù shàng zhāzhā de jiào.
example.english: The little bird chirps in the tree.
example.fact: In Qing-dynasty court dramas, officials are often shown responding to the emperor with a sharp '喳!' (zhā), a Manchu-influenced expression of respectful acknowledgment equivalent to 'yes, sir!'

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — the tree/wood radical, marking the character as related to trees, wood, or wooden objects.
陏 (a rare component, historically read close to duǒ) gives a sound close to 椭's reading tuǒ, sharing the same final, with initials d/t differing only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 地球绕太阳运行的轨道是椭圆形的。
example.pinyin: Dìqiú rào tàiyáng yùnxíng de guǐdào shì tuǒyuánxíng de.
example.english: The Earth's orbit around the sun is elliptical.
example.fact: Johannes Kepler discovered in the early 17th century that planetary orbits are ellipses, not perfect circles as previously believed — overturning nearly 2,000 years of astronomical assumption dating back to Aristotle and Ptolemy.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
米 (mǐ) gives a sound close to 咪's reading mī — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 小猫咪咪地叫着要吃饭。
example.pinyin: Xiǎo māo mīmī de jiàozhe yào chīfàn.
example.english: The little cat meows, wanting to be fed.
example.fact: 咪 is also used as a cute, informal suffix for 'cat' — 猫咪 (māomī) is one of the most common affectionate terms for 'kitty' in modern Mandarin, especially online.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — depicts rain falling from a cloud, marking the character as related to weather or precipitation.
妾 (qiè) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 霎's reading shà.

example.hanzi: 霎时间，天空下起了大雨。
example.pinyin: Shàshí jiān, tiānkōng xiàqǐ le dàyǔ.
example.english: In an instant, it began to rain heavily.
example.fact: 霎 combines the 'rain' radical 雨 with a phonetic element, reflecting its original meaning as a brief spell of rain — the sense of 'an instant' (霎时) grew from how quickly a passing drizzle comes and goes.

etymologyHint: As trustworthy 㐰 as spring-water 川

components.note: 亻 (person) marks the character as describing a person's character or behavior.

川 depicts a flowing river; paired with 'mouth' above it in the full character, it evokes words flowing smoothly and continuously — giving 侃 its meaning 'upright and forthright' and, in modern usage, 'to chat idly' (as in 侃大山, kǎn dàshān, 'to shoot the breeze').

example.hanzi: 他们几个人坐在一起侃大山。
example.pinyin: Tāmen jǐ gè rén zuò zài yīqǐ kǎn dàshān.
example.english: The group of them sat together chatting about nothing in particular.
example.fact: 侃大山 is Beijing-dialect slang for chatting casually, and 侃 alone has become common slang for 'to talk a lot,' a shift from its older, more formal meaning of 'upright and forthright.'

components.note: 犭 (animal) — the dog/animal radical, marking the character as related to an animal.
卒 (zú) gives a sound close to 猝's reading cù, sharing the same final, with initials z/c differing only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 这场意外让大家猝不及防。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng yìwài ràng dàjiā cùbùjífáng.
example.english: This accident caught everyone completely off guard.
example.fact: Sudden cardiac death (猝死) most often results from an abrupt disruption of the heart's electrical rhythm, and survival rates drop by roughly 10% for every minute that passes without defibrillation.

components.note: 穴 (cave) — depicts a cave or hole, marking the character as related to a hollow or enclosed space.
告 (gào) gives a sound close to 窖's reading jiào, sharing the same final.

example.hanzi: 这瓶酒已经窖藏了十年。
example.pinyin: Zhè píng jiǔ yǐjīng jiàocángle shí nián.
example.english: This bottle of wine has been cellar-aged for ten years.
example.fact: 窖藏 is a term frequently seen on Chinese liquor (baijiu) labels, referring to the traditional practice of aging spirits in underground pits or cellars, believed to mellow their flavor over time.

components.note: 戈 (dagger-axe) — depicts a dagger-axe, a bladed weapon on a pole, marking the character as related to combat.
翏 (liù) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 戮's reading lù.

example.hanzi: 战争带来了大规模的杀戮。
example.pinyin: Zhànzhēng dàiláile dàguīmó de shālù.
example.english: War brought about large-scale killing.
example.fact: In the classical idiom 戮力同心 ('to join forces and hearts together'), 戮 carries an older, unrelated sense of 'to combine effort' — a rare case where an idiom's meaning diverges sharply from a character's everyday meaning.

components.note: 礻 (spirit/altar) — a form of 示 (spirit, altar), marking the character as related to ritual, worship, or the supernatural.
司 (sī) gives a sound close to 祠's reading cí, sharing the same final, with s/c being closely related dental sibilant initials.

example.hanzi: 村里有一座古老的祠堂。
example.pinyin: Cūn lǐ yǒu yí zuò gǔlǎo de cítáng.
example.english: There is an old ancestral hall in the village.
example.fact: Ancestral halls (祠堂) historically served not just for ancestor worship but as centers of clan governance and education in southern China, some housing clan schools and administering local disputes.

components.note: 目 (eye) — the eye radical, marking the character as related to sight or the eyes.
属 (shǔ) gives a sound close to 瞩's reading zhǔ, sharing the same final, with initials sh/zh differing only in retroflex quality.

example.hanzi: 这场比赛引起了全球瞩目。
example.pinyin: Zhè chǎng bǐsài yǐnqǐle quánqiú zhǔmù.
example.english: This competition attracted global attention.
example.fact: 举世瞩目 ('the whole world's gaze is fixed upon it') is a common phrase in Chinese media for globally significant events, such as the Olympics or major space launches.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — the grass/plant radical, marking the character as related to plants or vegetation.
青 (qīng) gives a sound close to 菁's reading jīng, sharing the same final, with q/j a common alternation pair.

example.hanzi: 这本书汇集了作者一生的思想菁华。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū huìjíle zuòzhě yīshēng de sīxiǎng jīnghuá.
example.english: This book gathers the finest essence of the author's lifetime of thought.
example.fact: 菁 is used in the name of Jingtong (菁桐), a small scenic town in Taiwan's New Taipei City known for its old coal-mining railway and sky lantern festivals.

meanings: used in 躊躇|踌躇[chou2 chu2]

components.note: 足 (foot) — the foot radical, marking the character as related to the foot, legs, or walking.
著 (zhù, also zhe/zhuó) is the historical phonetic element; none of its readings closely match 躇's reading chú today.

example.hanzi: 他站在门口，踌躇不前。
example.pinyin: Tā zhàn zài ménkǒu, chóuchú bù qián.
example.english: He stood at the doorway, hesitating, unable to move forward.
example.fact: 踌躇 is an inseparable two-character binome in Chinese — neither 踌 nor 躇 has an independent meaning outside this compound, much like English 'topsy' and 'turvy' only make sense together.

etymologyHint: An old 老 person 亻; 老 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 亻 (person) marks this as referring to a person.
老 means 'old' and is pronounced lǎo — identical to 佬 — originally suggesting a mature man, now used more generally (often informally, or in Cantonese) for 'man, guy.'

example.hanzi: 他是村里有名的阔佬。
example.pinyin: Tā shì cūn lǐ yǒumíng de kuòlǎo.
example.english: He is the well-known rich man of the village.
example.fact: 佬 is a colloquial suffix describing a type of man, seen in words like 乡巴佬 ('country bumpkin') and, in Cantonese-influenced usage, 鬼佬 ('foreigner,' informal and sometimes considered impolite).

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — a form of 肉 (flesh, body), marking the character as related to a body part or bodily substance.
力 (lì) gives a sound close to 肋's reading lē, sharing the same initial consonant.

example.hanzi: 他穿得肋脦，一点也不整洁。
example.pinyin: Tā chuān de lēde, yìdiǎn yě bù zhěngjié.
example.english: He was dressed in a slovenly way, not tidy at all.
example.fact: 肋 is usually read lèi and means 'rib' (as in 肋骨), but this reading, lē, is much rarer and appears only in the northern dialect word 肋脦 (lēde), meaning 'slovenly' or 'unkempt.'

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the mouth radical, marking the character as related to speech, sound, or an action of the mouth.
出 (chū) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 咄's reading duō.

example.hanzi: 他说话咄咄逼人。
example.pinyin: Tā shuōhuà duōduōbìrén.
example.english: He speaks in an aggressive, overbearing way.
example.fact: The idiom 咄咄逼人 describes an intimidatingly aggressive manner of speech or behavior, rooted in this character's original sense as an exclamation of anger or command.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the heart radical, marking the character as related to emotions or mental states.
中 (zhōng) gives a sound close to 忡's reading chōng, sharing the same final, with initials zh/ch differing only in aspiration.

example.hanzi: 妈妈忧心忡忡地等着孩子回家。
example.pinyin: Māma yōuxīn chōngchōng de děngzhe háizi huí jiā.
example.english: Mom waited anxiously, deeply worried, for her child to come home.
example.fact: 忡 almost never appears alone in modern Mandarin — it survives essentially only in the fixed idiom 忧心忡忡, describing a state of persistent, heavy-hearted worry.

etymologyHint: Birds 乡 living together in a village 乡

components.note: 隹 depicts a short-tailed bird. The character's imagery of many birds gathering and calling together came to symbolize harmony and union.

example.hanzi: 她举止雍容大方。
example.pinyin: Tā jǔzhǐ yōngróng dàfang.
example.english: Her manner is dignified, graceful, and composed.
example.fact: Yongzheng (雍正, r. 1722–1735), the fourth Qing emperor, is known for major administrative and fiscal reforms that strengthened imperial finances ahead of his son Qianlong's long, prosperous reign.

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — the heart radical, marking the character as related to emotions or mental states.

冘 is a rare, ancient component also found in 沈/沉 (chén); despite carrying an independent reading of yín in some contexts, in this phonetic series it strongly cues the chén sound family, matching 忱's reading exactly.

example.hanzi: 他对工作充满热忱。
example.pinyin: Tā duì gōngzuò chōngmǎn rèchén.
example.english: He is full of enthusiasm for his work.
example.fact: 热忱 is a common word in formal Chinese recommendation letters, often paired with 工作 ('work') or 服务 ('service') to commend someone's dedicated, warm-hearted attitude.

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — the grass/plant radical, marking the character as related to plants or vegetation.
雷 (léi) gives a sound close to 蕾's reading lěi — the same syllable, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 春天，花蕾渐渐绽开。
example.pinyin: Chūntiān, huālěi jiànjiàn zhànkāi.
example.english: In spring, flower buds gradually bloom open.
example.fact: 蕾 is also used metaphorically in Chinese to describe a promising young person, as in 花蕾般的少女 ('a girl like a flower bud'), evoking untapped potential about to blossom.

components.note: 足 (foot) — the foot radical, marking the character as related to the foot, legs, or walking.
仓 (cāng) gives a sound close to 跄's reading qiāng, sharing the same final.

example.hanzi: 老人踉跄地走上楼梯。
example.pinyin: Lǎorén liàngqiàng de zǒushàng lóutī.
example.english: The elderly man staggered up the stairs.
example.fact: 踉跄 is another of Chinese's inseparable two-character binomes, where neither syllable carries independent meaning — the pair together conveys the unsteady, stumbling gait it describes.

components.note: 石 (stone) — the stone radical, marking the character as related to rock or stone.
圭 (guī) gives the sound — an exact match with 硅's reading.

example.hanzi: 美国的硅谷是全球科技创新的中心。
example.pinyin: Měiguó de Guīgǔ shì quánqiú kējì chuàngxīn de zhōngxīn.
example.english: America's Silicon Valley is a global center of tech innovation.
example.fact: Silicon is the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust after oxygen, and it's the essential material used to make the semiconductor chips that power nearly all modern electronics.

etymologyHint: A man 亻 who can support 支 someone

components.note: 亻 (person) marks the character as about a person.

支 means 'to support, a branch' and by extension 'a skill or ability'; combined with 'person,' it gave 伎 its meaning of a person with special talent or skill, historically used for skilled performers or entertainers.

example.hanzi: 他的伎俩被大家看穿了。
example.pinyin: Tā de jìliǎng bèi dàjiā kànchuān le.
example.english: Everyone saw through his tricks.
example.fact: 伎俩 today almost always carries a negative meaning, 'tricks' or 'schemes,' even though 伎 originally referred more neutrally to 'skill' or 'talent,' particularly that of trained performers.

components.note: 火 (fire) — the fire radical, marking the character as related to fire, heat, or burning.
欠 (qiàn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer closely matches 炊's reading chuī.

example.hanzi: 村庄上空升起了袅袅炊烟。
example.pinyin: Cūnzhuāng shàngkōng shēngqǐle niǎoniǎo chuīyān.
example.english: Wisps of cooking smoke rose above the village.
example.fact: 炊烟 (smoke rising from household cooking fires) is one of the most common images in Chinese poetry for evoking peaceful, rural domestic life.

etymologyHint: A metal 钅 knife 刂; 刂 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) points to metalworking, such as forging or sharpening a blade.
刂 is a form of 刀 (knife); the image of a sharpened blade extended metaphorically to 钊's meaning 'to strive, endeavor, encourage.' It's now mostly seen as a given-name character.

example.hanzi: 钊常用作男孩的名字，寓意努力奋进。
example.pinyin: Zhāo cháng yòngzuò nánhái de míngzi, yùyì nǔlì fènjìn.
example.english: Zhao is often used as a boy's name, symbolizing diligent effort and striving forward.
example.fact: 钊 appears in the name of Li Dazhao (李大钊, 1889–1927), one of the founders of the Chinese Communist Party and an early promoter of Marxist thought in China.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — the insect radical, originally depicting a snake-like shape, marking the character as related to insects or small creatures.
畐 (fú) gives the sound — an exact match with 蝠's reading; 畐 is the shared root behind other fú characters like 副 and 富.

example.hanzi: 蝙蝠是唯一会飞的哺乳动物。
example.pinyin: Biānfú shì wéiyī huì fēi de bǔrǔ dòngwù.
example.english: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
example.fact: Bats are indeed the only mammals capable of sustained flight — flying squirrels only glide. In Chinese culture, the bat is also a symbol of good fortune, because 蝠 (fú) sounds identical to 福 (fú, 'blessing').

meanings: (bound form) secretion (of the ear, eye etc)
etymologyHint: A person, crouched 尸 defecating 米; 米 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 尸 depicts a person in a bent or crouching posture (the same component used for 'corpse' and other body-related characters).
The small dots resembling grains of rice (米) represent what is expelled — combined with the crouching figure, giving 屎 its meaning 'excrement.'

example.hanzi: 地上有一堆狗屎，要小心。
example.pinyin: Dì shàng yǒu yì duī gǒushǐ, yào xiǎoxīn.
example.english: There's a pile of dog poop on the ground, be careful.
example.fact: Dung beetles can move dung many times their own body weight, and remarkably, some species navigate using the polarization pattern of moonlight and the Milky Way to travel in straight lines.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — the hand radical, marking the character as related to an action performed with the hand.
式 (shì) gives the sound — an exact match with 拭's reading.

example.hanzi: 他用毛巾擦拭桌子。
example.pinyin: Tā yòng máojīn cāshì zhuōzi.
example.english: He wipes the table with a towel.
example.fact: The idiom 拭目以待 ('to wipe one's eyes and wait') means to eagerly and expectantly await an outcome, evoking the image of clearing one's eyes so as not to miss it.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — a form of 言 (speech), marking the character as related to talking or language.
帝 (dì) gives the sound — an exact match with 谛's reading.

example.hanzi: 他终于领悟了生活的真谛。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú lǐngwùle shēnghuó de zhēndì.
example.english: He finally grasped the true meaning of life.
example.fact: In Buddhist philosophy, 谛 (Sanskrit: satya) denotes fundamental truths, most famously the 'Four Noble Truths' (四圣谛), the foundational teaching of the historical Buddha's first sermon.

etymologyHint: Th take off 退 clothing 衤; 退 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 衤 (clothing) marks the character as related to garments.
退 means 'to retreat, withdraw' and is pronounced tuì — identical to 褪 — combined with 'clothing' to mean pulling clothing off, and by extension, colors 'retreating' or fading.

example.hanzi: 这件衣服洗久了会褪色。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu xǐ jiǔ le huì tuìsè.
example.english: This piece of clothing will fade after being washed many times.
example.fact: Fabric dyes fade mainly because UV light breaks down the chemical bonds in dye molecules and repeated washing physically strips dye particles from fibers, which is why dark clothes are often washed inside-out in cold water.

components.note: 一 here is a simple horizontal stroke forming the ground-line of the character's ancient pictograph (not literally 'one') — part of an original image of a hand lifting a kneeling figure, which gave 丞 its meaning 'to assist, rescue.'
氶 (chéng) gives the sound — an exact match with 丞's reading; 氶 is in fact the ancient original form of 丞 itself.

example.hanzi: 丞相是古代皇帝之下最高的官员。
example.pinyin: Chéngxiàng shì gǔdài huángdì zhīxià zuìgāo de guānyuán.
example.english: The chancellor was the highest official below the emperor in ancient times.
example.fact: The office of chancellor (丞相) was one of the most powerful in imperial Chinese bureaucracy for centuries, until the Ming dynasty's founding emperor abolished it in 1380 after executing his own chancellor.

etymologyHint: Ten 十 different types of grass 艹

components.note: 艹 is the grass/plant radical. 卉's older form actually stacked three 屮 ('sprout') shapes together to symbolize a great variety of plants — giving 卉 its meaning 'flowers, plants in general.'

example.hanzi: 植物园里种着各种花卉。
example.pinyin: Zhíwùyuán lǐ zhòngzhe gèzhǒng huāhuì.
example.english: All kinds of flowers and plants are grown in the botanical garden.
